newsitem.title: USA: Lawmakers, White House prepare for new budget talks.
newsitem.headline: Lawmakers, White House prepare for new budget talks.

text.p: White House officials Wednesday said Republicans in Congress had moved to the right on key spending and tax issues, making it difficult to approve balanced budget legislation by August as planned.

Further complicating the outlook, President Clinton made a strong pitch for Congress to approve a 20-cents-per-pack increase in the federal cigarette tax to fund a children's health package and accused Republicans of watering down the children's benefits in their plan.
House Republicans balked at the tax boost, which passed the Senate, worried they will be unable to muster the votes for a long-sought tax-cutting measure if it is included.
White House officials and Democrats met Wednesday with congressional Republicans, who spent the past several days working out new bargaining positions on taxes and spending.

After meeting on Medicare, Medicaid and other programmes, White House budget director Franklin Raines said Republicans put new issues on the table that would be tough to resolve by Aug. 1, the goal for sending a bill to the White House.

"We only have nine days in which to move from a large number of issues to a bill the president can sign," Raines said. "There are new issues on the table that weren't there yesterday and the day before."
He said Republicans had moved as far away as possible from welfare agreements contained in an initial five-year balanced budget deal between Congress and the White House.
Republicans rejected key parts of a White House plan continuing disability aid to legal immigrants who will lose benefits this summer under a new welfare law.

"If everybody works together, there will have to be some give and take, but I think we can come up with a good bill that can pass both houses and be signed by the president," said Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth, Republican of Delaware.

Earlier Wednesday Senate Democratic leader Tom Daschle, of South Dakota, said flatly the proposed Republican bill was "veto bait," saying it was impossible for the president or Democrats to support the package.
The Republican compromise includes a White House-opposed provision to index capital gains for inflation. Republicans also offered a revised plan for a $500-per-child tax credit.

The White House said it wanted to ensure low-income workers received the full credit, even if they got a separate tax break designed to supplement wages. Republicans said families who do not pay income taxes should not get the credit.
The new structure would allow the child credit to be put in a special account for up to three years for low-income workers until they reached a point where they owed income tax.

House and Senate Republicans could not agree on a Senate-passed plan to increase the federal cigarette tax to raise about $15 billion over five years. About $8 billion would be used to help fund a children's health initiative that already has $16 billion earmarked in the budget bill.
"This 20-cent increase in the cigarette tax not only will provide necessary resources to protect and improve children's health ... It is the right thing to do," Clinton said.

Aside from the tax question, the White House and lawmakers were at odds over other aspects of the children's health plan. Republicans proposed giving states block grants to use either for either insurance or for direct services. Clinton said the benefits Republicans proposed were not comprehensive and he called on lawmakers to beef up their proposal.
